article.excerpt: What if you could become anyone? With Kling AI's Motion Control, you can transfer any video movement to any image. This guide covers everything from basic dance videos to advanced parameter tuning and model comparisons.

content_sections.heading: Opening Hook
content_sections.content:
What if you could become anyone? A boxer throwing punches in a neon-lit street. A dancing monk in flowing robes. A chimp grooving to music in sunglasses. With Kling AI's Motion Control feature, you can take any video movement and apply it to any image—transforming static pictures into dynamic, living videos.

This guide walks you through everything from your first motion transfer to advanced parameter tuning and model comparisons. By the end, you'll have the prompts, settings, and know-how to create professional-quality motion videos.

content_sections.heading: TL;DR
content_sections.content: Kling AI's Motion Control transfers movements from any video to any image. Use **Partial mode** for mismatched framings, **Standard mode** for testing, and **Pro mode** for final renders. Kling 2.6 beats Runway and OpenArt in both quality and price.

content_sections.caption: Main tutorial video showcasing Kling Motion Control

content_sections.heading: What is Motion Control?
content_sections.content: **Motion Control** is a feature in Kling AI's Video 2.6 model that transfers body movements and facial expressions from a reference video onto a target image. Unlike traditional video generation that creates motion from text prompts alone, Motion Control uses an actual video as the motion source—giving you precise control over every movement.
key_capabilities: Transfer dance moves, gestures, or any body motion
Preserve facial expressions and lip sync
Apply movements to humans, animals, or stylized characters
Work with any image style: realistic, anime, cyberpunk, Renaissance paintings

content_sections.heading: Case 1: Getting Started — Dance Videos
content_sections.description: The easiest way to learn Motion Control is with a simple dance video.
workflow_steps: Open Kling AI — Navigate to the Kling AI web interface
Select Video — Click on the Video tab
Choose Model — Select the Video 2.6 model (latest version)
Select Motion Control — Click the Motion Control tab
Upload Reference Video — Choose a video with single character, smooth movements, good lighting
Upload Target Image — Select the character you want to animate
Add Prompt (Optional) — Describe the scene for better results
Click Generate — Wait for your video to render

prompt_template.format: A [style] [character] is dancing [dance type] in [location], [lighting], [shot type]
prompt_template.example: A Shaolin monk is dancing hip-hop in a temple courtyard, golden hour lighting, full body shot

content_sections.heading: Case 2: Level Up — Complex Motion Transfer
content_sections.description: Fast-paced boxing movements with motion blur. This is where understanding Kling's parameters becomes essential.
content_sections.scenario: Shadow boxing video—quick punches, body rotation, rapid arm movements. Target: A cyberpunk girl in a neon street.

parameters.name: Motion Reference Control
parameters.description: How closely to follow the source video

parameters.name: Original Sound
parameters.description: Whether to preserve audio from source

exact.description: Tries to replicate the source video precisely
exact.best_for: When your image framing matches the video framing
exact.issues: Can cause problems if aspect ratios differ; character may get cut off

partial.description: Gives the AI flexibility to adapt movements
partial.benefits: Keeps camera more stable, often produces more natural results

content_sections.pro_tip: Standard mode sometimes produces better motion than Pro, even at lower resolution. Test both—you can always upscale a good Standard result.

prompt_template.example: A cyberpunk girl is shadow boxing in the street, dynamic motion, cinematic lighting

content_sections.heading: Prompt Guide: The 7-Element Framework

templates.format: A [style] [character] is dancing [dance style] in [location], [lighting], [shot type]
A [style] [character] is talking/singing in [location], expressive face, [emotion]

content_sections.note: You can leave the prompt blank and let the AI interpret the motion, but adding a prompt typically improves consistency and style.

questions.question: Can I use Motion Control with animals?
questions.answer: Yes. Testing shows excellent results with animals like chimps and cats. The key is matching the body shape roughly to the reference video's subject. A portrait-style monkey image with a human reference video works surprisingly well.

questions.question: What if my background goes crazy?
questions.answer: This sometimes happens, especially with Exact mode and high-motion videos. Try Partial mode, which tends to keep backgrounds more stable. Also consider adding background description to your prompt.

questions.question: Should I always use Pro mode?
questions.answer: Not necessarily. Standard mode sometimes produces better motion quality, just at lower resolution. Do a test run in Standard first—if the motion looks good, you can either use it or try Pro for the final render.

questions.question: Why doesn't Runway detect my face?
questions.answer: Runway Act 2 seems more restrictive about face detection. If it fails, try Kling or OpenArt Motion instead, as they're more flexible with different character types.

questions.question: Can I do lip sync with any face?
questions.answer: Lip sync works best with human or human-like faces, clear front-facing views, and images that match the framing of your speaking video. Results vary with stylized characters—realistic faces give the most natural lip sync.

content_sections.heading: Next Steps
action_plan: Start simple — Pick a slow, clear dance video as your reference
Match the framing — Choose an image with similar composition
Test both modes — Try Exact and Partial to see what works
Use Standard first — Save Pro mode for final renders
Iterate on prompts — Add details to improve consistency
content_sections.final_message:
The best way to master Motion Control is through experimentation. Every image and video combination behaves differently—what works for a cyberpunk boxer might not work for a dancing cat. But that's part of the creative fun.

Now go become anyone you want.
